item.title: Running Docker through WSL instead of Docker Desktop cut my resource usage in half, but there's a catch
item.itunes:title: Running Docker through WSL instead of Docker Desktop cut my resource usage in half, but there's a catch
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Using Docker Desktop meant never having to open a terminal or command prompt on Windows 11. I enjoyed that convenience until I opened the Task Manager to check something and learned that the app’s helper processes were using over a GB of memory on my desktop. And I wasn’t even building or serving anything. I had assumed that stopping a container released the resources.

That’s not how things work on Windows 11. The operating system runs a virtualization layer that Linux never needs, and Docker Desktop stacks another on top of that, especially since I had started using WSL2 for most tasks. I wanted to know how much overhead Docker Desktop actually needed. So I removed it from my desktop and ran the same container stack through WSL2.

Microsoft is baking Linux containers into Windows, and it might end my reliance on Docker Desktop

Linux containerization is now a default feature

5
By  Ty Sherback

Docker Desktop kept working in the background

Running two virtualization layers for a single container

I assumed Docker Desktop was like any other app, but the moment I opened the Task Manager, it turned out to be more than a tray icon. I found several backend engine processes, a networking helper called vpnkit, and a credential manager on that list. The surprising part was that those things were running even when there was no active container. Resource Saver trims some of this when nothing’s running, but it doesn’t make everything vanish. All those processes pop back the moment I open the dashboard or build a new container.

This happens because Docker Desktop sets up its own Linux distributions when I install it and uses them every time I open the app. One hosts the actual engine, the other stores images, containers, and volumes. Checking my list of WSL distros confirmed it: docker-desktop and docker-desktop-data sat right alongside Ubuntu, the distro I actually use.

Meanwhile, Windows already runs a lightweight VM to make WSL2 work, and Docker Desktop runs a second one inside that VM to host its engine. So I am running two virtualization layers to do what a single shared kernel would handle as a few isolated processes on real Linux. Well, that’s the deal I signed up for when I installed it. I didn’t realize how much it was costing me until I checked.

Running containers directly through WSL2 changed everything

Noticeably lighter on resources for the same workload

I switched my approach to see whether that overhead was actually necessary. I installed Docker’s engine directly in my Ubuntu WSL and skipped the Docker Desktop installer entirely. I ran Docker's official installation script to deploy it inside my WSL distro. After that, I deployed my usual stack of containers like Jellyfin, a Caddy proxy, Postgres, and Syncthing. Then I let those containers run for a couple of hours before checking memory usage in Task Manager.

The difference wasn’t subtle, since Docker Desktop already used over a GB of memory before I started a single container. In contrast, the same stack running in a plain WSL distro added only a few hundred MB on top of an idle installation. Docker Desktop’s background processes kept waking up the CPU even when nothing needed them to. The WSL2 setup stayed silent unless a container was actively running a task. Cutting out the second virtualization layer meant the WSL2 VM only had to do the work once instead of twice.

Speed was never the real problem

Idle overhead matters more than boot time

Because of everything the GUI does behind the scenes, it’s easy to assume that Docker Desktop is slower. Even with the native WSL setup, the container tooling still showed similar startup times. Some containers loaded faster, but that didn’t change how I work with them.

I was more concerned about the overhead that piles up after running containers all day than about the extra second or two of boot time. Once my container boots and isn’t used actively, it sits idle for hours. That idle time is what actually costs you resources, not the boot itself. I hadn’t measured that before, and it turned out to matter more than anything else.

Dropping Docker Desktop still has some trade-offs

Choosing the terminal over the dashboard comes at a price

Removing Docker Desktop isn’t a clean win because I miss the dashboard view of every container, image, and volume at a glance. Docker Desktop lets me start or stop containers with a single click. Meanwhile, I now manage that stack through the terminal. That’s not a big deal if you’re already familiar with the command line. But a GUI helps if you want friendlier options.

One inconvenience I face is setting up file sharing. Using Docker Desktop on Windows 11 makes it easy to set up the target folders from the app’s settings. I need to point to the folders. In contrast, I need to manually reference paths across Windows and WSL since it doesn’t pick that up automatically. It got a little irksome that I could no longer run Docker commands from any terminal, something Windows integration used to handle automatically.

Docker Desktop wired that up in the background so that I could use PowerShell or Command Prompt. On one hand, I save resources, but on the other, I’m limited to manually configuring things for a specific terminal.

I tested dual-boot, WSL2, and VMs to run Linux apps on Windows, and only one was worth keeping

Dual-boot, VMs, and WSL2 walk into a Windows PC...

10
By  Ayush Pande

Is Docker Desktop still worth keeping around?

Yes, I’ve decided to keep it around. Most of my containers run continuously on a machine that’s rarely doing anything else. The difference between one virtualization layer and two adds up daily. If your workflow involves active development sessions, then it’s worth keeping Docker Desktop around. The dashboard’s convenience is worth the extra memory Docker Desktop uses. I keep Docker Desktop installed for the one project that needs its GUI. Everything else that runs long-term lives inside a plain WSL2 distro.

Docker Desktop is a one-click-install application for your Mac, Linux, or Windows environment that lets you build, share, and run containerized applications and microservices. It provides a straightforward GUI (Graphical User Interface) that lets you manage your containers, applications, and images directly from your machine.
Docker Desktop reduces the time spent on complex setups so you can focus on writing code. It takes care of port mappings, file system concerns, and other default settings, and is regularly updated with bug fixes and security updates.

item.title: I turned off a few key settings, and my old TV suddenly felt almost new again
item.itunes:title: I turned off a few key settings, and my old TV suddenly felt almost new again
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have got a fairly old smart TV, not the archaic kind, but it's about 4-5 years old. And over time, I noticed it slowed down a bit, as is the case with any device. Even our smartphones and computers slow down after a few years. For the longest time, I ignored it because I just assumed that TVs have less powerful processors and don't always age as gracefully.

While part of that is true, I recently discovered that turning off a few settings and adjusting others can noticeably improve performance. Remember, the goal is to minimize background activity — things that are non-essential but still consume a significant share of the system's resources. This means that you can go beyond what the list covers — it's not comprehensive by any means — as long as you understand the upsides and downsides of the change.

Automatic Content Recognition

It's good for privacy too

Automatic Content Recognition, or ACR, is something very few people actually know about, but once they do, they instantly disable it, and not just for performance gains. ACR, as the name suggests, is a feature that monitors what's happening on the screen, the kind of content you are watching, in real time. The data is then shared with the manufacturer, who can use it in multiple ways, whether to serve targeted ads or sell it to third parties.

That's why disabling ACR also helps protect your privacy. Not every manufacturer labels the feature the same way. For instance, Samsung TVs call it Viewing Information Services, while Sony TVs label it Samba Interactive TV. You'll usually find the option to turn off ACR under Advertising or Privacy settings. Also, if you are using a streaming stick like Roku or Fire TV Stick, make sure to disable any similar settings there as well.

Your smart TV is screenshotting everything you watch, but here's how to block it

Your seemingly innocent smart TV may be tracking more than you think, and a few privacy settings can shut down the worst of it.

2
By  Jeff Butts

Motion Smoothing

It's not for everyone, but it's still worth considering

Motion smoothing is another feature I disabled on my smart TV. It adds extra frames to the content to make things look smoother. Motion smoothing comes into play because the content you usually watch is filmed at a lower frame rate (24-30fps) than your TV's refresh rate (60–120 fps or higher), and it tries to match that. That's some extra effort your TV is putting in for something not everyone necessarily benefits from.

Disabling motion smoothing is simple, though, since every manufacturer labels the feature differently. For instance, it can be called TruMotion, Auto Motion Plus, or Action Smoothing, but you'll usually find it under the Picture or Display settings. Motion smoothing can help when you are watching sports, but for movies and shows, you are generally better off without it.

Your TV's motion smoothing isn't the only setting ruining movies

Fix your TV's settings in a few clicks and watch movies the way they were meant to be seen.

By  Patrick Hearn

Autoplay and animations

Minimize unnecessary activity as much as you can

Two other things that actively consume resources in the background without providing any real benefit are autoplay and animations. Autoplay refers to automatic audio and video previews and adds little value to the overall experience. On the contrary, the feature can sometimes make your experience less than pleasant. On Fire TV, you will find autoplay in Preferences under Featured Content, while on Google TV, it's within the Accounts and Profile settings.

The same goes for animations. You get little value from them, and on older TVs or models with less powerful processors, animations can slow things down. To turn off animations on an Android TV, first enable Developer Options. From here, you disable them under Transition Animation Scale.

I blocked my smart TV from reaching the internet, and it actually loads apps faster now

Making the TV actually smart.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

Energy saver

The increase in power consumption is barely noticeable

This is something worth looking into if your TV feels somewhat slow or laggy, or the picture quality doesn't seem as vibrant. As the name suggests, Energy Saver is a feature designed to lower your TV's power consumption, and it does so by adjusting the picture quality, or the brightness and contrast, to be precise.

Disabling Energy Saver may or may not directly impact performance on every TV, but you should still disable it. Modern TVs don't consume as much electricity as you might think, so the feature is redundant. If you really want to save money on power bills, set up energy automations in Home Assistant.

6 settings I always change to make any TV feel more premium

You can extract way more out of your TV than you realize

5
By  Tanveer Singh

Clear cache

You should do it periodically

Though not a setting, this is by far the most effective way to improve the performance of an old TV or even speed up an old Fire TV Stick. For those of you who don't know, apps create a cache to improve loading times and speed things up. But as the cache size grows, your TV has less free storage. The cache can also get cluttered or corrupted, which can trigger slowdowns and errors.

I clear my smart TV's cache and each app's cache every few months. That's because this is not a one-time thing; the apps rebuild the cache over time. You shouldn't overdo it either, as it will prove counterproductive.

Why I stopped buying smart TVs, and what I bought instead

Remember when smart features worked for us, instead of against us?

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

With the right settings in place, you can defer the upgrade

If you have been planning to ditch your old TV and upgrade to a new one, I recommend reconfiguring its settings and disabling any non-essential features that are eating up resources. It won't make your TV as fast as it was when new, but with minimal background processes, it will feel faster. The best part is that none of it drastically affects the picture quality.

item.title: 4 things Raycast on Windows does that PowerToys Run still can't
item.itunes:title: 4 things Raycast on Windows does that PowerToys Run still can't
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I still remember installing Microsoft PowerToys for the first time a couple of years ago just because I wanted to replace Windows Search with something simpler. At the time, I just wanted to get away from unnecessary web results and Start menu recommendations when I tried to open an app. But then, when Raycast rolled out on Windows as a beta last year, I decided to give it a shot since I used to rely on it quite a bit on my MacBook Air. Now that it's finally available as a stable build, I feel more comfortable talking about it.

On the surface, Raycast and PowerToys Run are similar: you can use them to launch apps, find files, or do calculations. But to know how capable Raycast really is, you need to stop treating it like a search box because it's packed with features that let you get things done without leaving the launcher. And the fact that I can just use the Windows key to bring it up instead of a separate keyboard shortcut makes it feel much more like a proper replacement for Windows Search.

I replaced Windows Search and I’ve never been happier

Nobody likes Windows Search

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Raycast has AI built right in

And the integration is actually well thought out

In 2026, you're probably not even surprised that a third-party launcher has AI integration, but I really like how Raycast has gone about it. Sure, you can open AI Chat and use it like pretty much any other chatbot, with plenty of models to choose from. But that's the least interesting part. Quick AI lets me type queries without leaving the launcher, which is perfect for those one-off questions. In fact, I haven't had to open the full interface even once.

The best part about Raycast's implementation, though, is Screen Awareness, which uses whatever I'm looking at as context. For instance, if I want a summary of an article I'm reading, I can bring up Raycast and just type "summarize this article" instead of copying and pasting the whole thing. I've even used it to summarize YouTube videos when I'm short on time. You also have things like Quick Fix to fix spelling and grammar, AI Commands for repeated prompts, and AI Extensions to connect it to apps you use. Raycast AI is only available on the Pro plan, which costs $8/month, but you do get a 7-day free trial to see if it's worth it.

Snippets are a huge time-saver

You don't have to type the same things over and over

This is a feature I didn't really care much about until recently. Think of Snippets as text replacement on an iPhone or a Mac. You create a snippet inside Raycast, give it a name, save the text you want it to insert, and then assign a keyword if you want it to expand automatically without opening the launcher every time. You can have paragraphs of text saved inside a single snippet, so you're not limited to simple things like an email address or a URL.

This is perfect if you're someone who sends the same kind of emails every day at work. And you can even use dynamic placeholders for things like the current date, time, and whatever you have copied to your clipboard, so a snippet can change depending on when you use it. You can also choose where the cursor ends up after the text expands, which is handy if there's a part you need to fill in manually every time, like someone's name.

Quicklinks are shortcuts that do more

You can use them to open websites, files, and content inside apps

It's easy to assume Quicklinks are basically just bookmarks that I can access through Raycast, but they're quite a bit more useful than that. Besides websites, you can point them to files and folders you regularly open, or even specific content inside an app. For instance, instead of opening Spotify and finding a playlist yourself, you can create a Quicklink that takes you straight there from Raycast.

You can create one by searching for Create Quicklink in Raycast. Give it a name, enter the link or path you want to open, and choose the app you want Raycast to open it with. If you're already on the webpage you want to save, Raycast can fill in the URL for you. Like Snippets, it supports dynamic placeholders, so you can have it automatically use things like text from your clipboard when opening a Quicklink. You can also add arguments, meaning you can create a Quicklink for YouTube, type whatever you want to search for directly into Raycast, and have it take you straight to the results.

The Extension Store is the final piece

Because it connects Raycast to even more apps and services

At this point, you probably already have a good idea of how much more capable Raycast is than PowerToys Run on its own, but the Extension Store is the icing on the cake. You can find hundreds of community-built extensions for third-party apps like Notion, Slack, Spotify, 1Password, and more. Depending on the extension, you can search for content, trigger actions, or pull information without opening the app first.

It's not as extensive as Raycast for Mac, but considering the Windows version has only been around for a year, I'm still very impressed. You can search for extensions directly in the launcher after opening Store or browse through them on Raycast's website. Once you install an extension, its commands will show up alongside everything else in Raycast, so you don't really have to think of them as separate add-ons. PowerToys Run, on the other hand, has plugins, but you have to dig through GitHub repos and install them manually, so it's not really comparable to a dedicated store.

PowerToys narrows the gap with Command Palette, though

To be fair, PowerToys Run is outdated at this point, and Microsoft has already started pushing users toward Command Palette. It's basically the future of PowerToys Run since it closes some of the gaps I've talked about here. Extension Gallery and Bookmarks are Command Palette's equivalents of the Extension Store and Quicklinks, respectively. So, if you're already using PowerToys, I'd definitely try Command Palette before switching to Raycast. I've used Command Palette for a while myself, but I still think Raycast has the edge with its AI integration and Snippets. So, unless Microsoft adds these features down the line, I don't see myself going back to it anytime soon.

item.title: I ditched my Synology NAS for a UGREEN, and the processing power alone makes it worth it
item.itunes:title: I ditched my Synology NAS for a UGREEN, and the processing power alone makes it worth it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's been a while since my NAS was just the spot where I stored data. Between Docker containers, self-hosted services, backups, and, of course, media, what I want from the hardware has changed a lot. While my Synology has been a solid companion, I've been on the lookout for something a bit more powerful. Something with a bit more grunt under the hood.

So, I decided to check out the UGREEN DXP4800 Pro. I still wanted an appliance-style device, which, to me, made a NAS the obvious choice. This UGREEN NAS has the hardware to function as a small home server while still performing all standard NAS functions. After using it for a bit, I can say there's a lot to like here. But also a few things that I'm not too convinced by. Read on to find out.

I turned this NAS into a Proxmox home server, and TrueNAS inside a VM solved my biggest storage problem

Turns out, a Proxmox and TrueNAS hybrid storage server works exceedingly well

By  Ayush Pande

It feels more like a small home server than a NAS

More processing power gives self-hosted tools room to breathe

Look, Synology devices have never been known for their top-end performance. But the gulf between what UGREEN offers and Synology's options is astonishingly wide. The DXP4800 Pro is equipped with an Intel Core i3-1315U processor and 8GB of DDR5 RAM out of the box. Of course, you can upgrade the latter if you choose. For the kind of use cases I and most homelabbers are putting our NAS boxes through, that beefy-by-NAS-standards processor is a much better fit.

Docker is a big part of my self-hosting setup, and I've gradually built up a substantial collection of self-hosted applications. Running those directly on the NAS means I don't need a separate computer dedicated to keeping them up and running. UGREEN's UGOS Pro also offers native Docker support. Now, that part isn't very surprising, and I'd still end up using something like Portainer for more control. However, even as a basic application, the Docker implementation is much more robust than what Synology offers in its ability to use Compose files and more.

Combined with the extra processing power, the DXP4800 Pro gives me more room to spin up performance-intensive containers, more containers in general, or even a combination of the two.

High-speed networking

10GbE makes moving large files much faster

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

The other major upgrade with the DXP4800 Pro is the networking speed. The device has a 10GbE network port alongside a 2.5GbE port. Look, I'll be the first one to tell you that I don't need 10-gig networking for most tasks. Opening a document or a photograph doesn't get a speed bump with 10GbE networking. But that's not all my NAS does.

Anytime I'm moving large amounts of data between machines, 10GbE networking gives me the bandwidth to move it seamlessly and much faster than I otherwise could. Lately, it's been useful as I consolidate data scattered around machines. Moreover, 10-gig networking is convenient, and it is another element of future-proofing. After all, most people don't just upgrade their NAS every few years. This is a device that you're expected to use for years to come.

I still miss some things from my Synology

Not having an equivalent to Synology's SHR is a big loss

The biggest downside of moving away from Synology is SHR, or the lack of an equivalent on the UGREEN. Synology Hybrid RAID is one of those feature additions you don't truly appreciate until you no longer have access to it.

Sure, UGREEN supports conventional RAID configurations including RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10, as well as Basic and JBOD, but there's no equivalent of SHR, and that's a big miss. Over time, I've accumulated drives of different capacities. With SHR, I had more flexibility when putting those drives to work.

Moreover, in times of exceptionally high hard drive prices, SHR let me upgrade drives one at a time. No such flexibility here. Moving to conventional RAID means I have to be a lot more deliberate about which drives I use and how I build my storage pool.

It's not necessarily a big concern if you're buying the NAS and a matching set of hard drives. But if your plan is to build up the storage over time, you'll have to plan right from the outset.

There's also the software. UGOS Pro is not bad at all. It has all the core features you could want, including storage management, file management, Docker and VM support. But you can't beat the years of refinement Synology has put into DSM. UGOS Pro, in comparison, feels like a work in progress with occasional buggy rendering or weird language translations. That maturity that only comes with age can't be speedrun. Today, this isn't a big deal for me as I self-host my own third-party software alternatives. But if you want software that has been tested trial-by-fire style, Synology would still be my choice.

A NAS more suited to my needs

I haven't entirely left the Synology ecosystem. In fact, I have plenty of Synology boxes still serving up files across my home network. But as my requirements change, the DXP4800 Pro is clearly more suited to the task. I need somewhere to keep my media and photos, but also something that can run services, host containers, and give me enough hardware headroom to experiment without needing another server. That's where the DXP4800 Pro has the leg up over Synology's offerings. After all, software can always be fixed or upgraded; hardware can't.

item.title: The unused USB ports on your Home Assistant server can do more than you think
item.itunes:title: The unused USB ports on your Home Assistant server can do more than you think
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Although Home Assistant’s terrific IoT paraphernalia management provisions and automation capabilities are worth highlighting, what I really love about this smart home platform is the sheer amount of ways I can customize it. The templates for deploying FOSS services within the app store alone make it possible to extend HASS’ functionality by bringing support for NVR solutions, ESP32 calibration tools, AI services, and a bunch of other utilities. That’s before I even mention the sheer number of wacky and ingenious integrations available on the Home Assistant Community Store.

That said, Home Assistant isn’t just customizable on the software front. I’ve often seen folks rock Home Assistant hosts with a handful of unoccupied USB ports. And let me tell you, there’s no shortage of cool USB gizmos you can pair with your HASS server to boost its functionality.

I gave Home Assistant access to my NAS, and it became the dashboard my smart home was missing

And that's before you include the cool automations I can create with this setup

1
By  Ayush Pande

External drives are surprisingly useful for bare-metal Home Assistant setups

Backups, database operations, camera footage – everything’s fair game for these drives

Back when I had a bare-metal Home Assistant server running on a cheap N100 mini-PC, I had a little bit of a problem with the backups. Since I didn’t have the handy Proxmox VM snapshots as I do now, I had to rely on local backups, which could easily get lost if something went wrong with the old SSD powering the mini-PC. As such, I added a direct-cheap external SSD to Home Assistant and configured the automated backups to use it as the storage drive. That way, I wouldn’t risk choking the underlying boot drive with frequent backups. Nor would I have to worry about my precious HASS configs, automations, apps, blueprints, and integrations getting lost if the boot drive kicked the bucket.

The same holds true for footage from security cameras. Although I rely on a separate Frigate instance for NVR detection, hosting this platform (or even motionEye) directly on a Home Assistant server would cause it to occupy large chunks of space every time a new footage gets saved. Heck, even if you don’t rely on either NVR utility and just stick to FFMPEG cameras hooked up to Home Assistant, it wouldn’t take too long for all the footage to start choking up the boot drive. Connecting an external drive to HASS and forcing the platform to save all screenshots and videos to it can help out a lot in this situation, and you could go down the HDD route to save some extra bucks on an SSD.

Although it’s not all that important for folks relying on modern SSDs for their Home Assistant boot pool, having a cheap drive handle the intensive logging and database write tasks can slow down the boot drive’s wear rate – and this is something I often did with dirt-cheap flash drives for my microSD card-powered Raspberry Pi HASS instance.

6 HACS integrations that combine my self-hosted services with Home Assistant

Smart devices aren't the only things I control with my Home Assistant server

By  Ayush Pande

But USB adapters are what you’re really looking for

With all the IoT protocols out there, you’re bound to need a few of these adapters

Switching from external drives to full-on USB adapters that I still use with my Home Assistant server, most PCs don’t support common communication standards that you’d find on smart devices. Even good ol’ Bluetooth might not be available on old PCs and thin clients, and considering the sheer number of cool gizmos that only support this standard, you’d be doing your Home Assistant hub a disservice if you only relied on Wi-Fi connectivity for your smart devices.

Tossing a USB Bluetooth adapter into the mix is all you need to bring these devices to Home Assistant. Between smart toothbrushes, fitness trackers, and measuring scales, you might end up finding several devices on your Home Assistant’s integration page when you finally arm it with a USB adapter.

While some mini-PCs might ship with Bluetooth functionality, I can’t say the same for Zigbee, Z-wave, and Thread protocols. And with more devices relying on these channels for local communication instead of Wi-Fi, I’d recommend picking up their respective adapters. Of course, you might not even need all of them depending on your specific smart devices. But at the very least, I’d recommend bringing Zigbee support to your HASS instance, as it’s a popular standard for modern IoT paraphernalia, and you don’t need to shell out a lot of money on its adapters.

I use a Home Assistant virtual machine running on top of Proxmox, and I had no issues connecting all these adapters to my HASS server once I configured USB passthrough. If you’re fond of ESP32 or Raspberry Pi Pico boards, I’d recommend leaving a spare USB port for microcontroller projects. Yes, I’m aware that ESPHome Device Builder lets you flash microcontrollers even when they’re hooked up to the client machine running the HASS web UI. But for projects such as radio co-processors, you’ll want to use a USB port on the Home Assistant host.

USB devices become even more useful once you go down the home server route

Besides Home Assistant, typical self-hosting workstations and virtualization rigs benefit from USB gizmos. A DAS, for example, can serve as a nice alternative to expensive NAS solutions when all you want to do is archive TBs of data and aren’t all that concerned about the file-sharing aspects of a centralized storage server. Likewise, USB-to-Ethernet adapters can be a decent investment if your server rig has a broken Ethernet port but doesn’t include dedicated PCIe slots where you can plug NICs.

item.title: I ditched my broken clipboard workflow for a sidebar that actually keeps up with how I work
item.itunes:title: I ditched my broken clipboard workflow for a sidebar that actually keeps up with how I work
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I copy a ridiculous number of things while working. A useful link from a browser, a sentence from an article, a screenshot, or a file I need in another app can all end up in my clipboard within minutes. The problem starts when I need those things later. I used to treat every copy as a quick transaction: copy it, use it, move on. That worked until I started handling several things at once. I wanted something that could keep up without making my workflow more complicated. That's when I came across Edge Drop, and it changed how I deal with copied content.

What is Edge Drop?

My copied stuff finally has a home

Edge Drop is a clipboard utility for Windows that gives me a dedicated place to keep the things I copy. After installing it, I get a slim bar along the edge of my display that opens into the clipboard panel when I move my mouse over it.

The app can handle different kinds of content, including text, links, images, screenshots, and files. This is useful because I don't have to think of my clipboard as being limited to plain text. I can use it for the different types of content that come up during my workday. The panel also gives me a quick view of what I've collected, with controls for individual items. I can preview content, copy it again, pin something important, or remove it when I'm done.

It makes clipboard management effortless

I can copy things without immediately pasting them

The biggest change for me was that I no longer have to think about pasting something the moment I copy it. Edge Drop gives me more breathing room. I can copy something and simply leave it there while I continue working. If I'm researching a topic, for example, I can collect several useful links without opening each one immediately. The same applies to snippets of text I might want to reference later.

I particularly like this when I'm writing. I can gather information first and decide what I actually need afterward, instead of constantly interrupting my writing to paste every item. It sounds like a small change, but it removes a surprising amount of mental overhead. I'm no longer trying to remember which item I copied most recently or worrying that copying something new will replace something I still need. I can keep working and deal with those copied items when the right moment comes.

This free and open-source self-hosted app syncs your clipboard across all of your devices

Say goodbye to the hassle of transferring text

5
By  Anurag Singh

Dragging files and links feels much better

Drag, drop, and get back to work

The part of Edge Drop I use most often is the drag-and-drop interaction. Once I have something sitting in the panel, I don't have to copy it again or figure out where it is in my clipboard history. I can just grab it and move it where I need it.

This works particularly well with files and links. If I have a file ready to use in another folder, I can drag it out instead of opening multiple windows just to move it around. The same feels natural with links. I can pick one up and drop it into the window where I want to use it.

What I like is that the action feels visual. I can see the item I'm moving, grab it, and place it where it belongs. There is less guesswork involved, especially when I have several things to work with. It turns a basic clipboard action into something that feels much closer to moving an actual object around my desktop.

It feels modern

Built for everyday work

What surprised me after using Edge Drop was how naturally it fit into my daily work. I didn't have to change the way I organize my desktop or build a new routine around the app. After a short while, using it started to feel normal.

I think that says a lot about good utility software. I don't want another application demanding my attention throughout the day. I want something that solves a small problem and then lets me carry on with the work that actually matters.

Edge Drop also feels refreshingly focused. It doesn't give me the impression that I need to explore every corner of the app to get value from it. I can understand what it's for almost immediately and start using it without much of a learning curve.

The clipboard is more than you might think

By  João Carrasqueira

My clipboard finally stopped getting in the way

I didn't expect a small utility to change such a routine part of my work, but Edge Drop has earned a permanent spot on my PC. The real benefit isn't having another app installed; it's having fewer moments where I have to stop and think about what I just copied. If you regularly move information between apps, files, and projects, this is one of those tools that makes more sense the longer you use it. For me, that's enough reason to keep it around.

item.title: My first ESP32 sensor solved a real problem, and now I'm building new projects every week
item.itunes:title: My first ESP32 sensor solved a real problem, and now I'm building new projects every week
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
In my early ESP32 tinkering days, I’d only use the microcontroller to test with LEDs, resistors, and other circuitry components. In fact, writing simple C++ programs to perform basic tasks on the ESP32 was the farthest I’d go with this microcontroller. And even then, my entire motivation behind tinkering with ESP32 templates on Arduino IDE was to get some first-hand experience with coding.

It wasn’t until I chanced upon the ESPHome Device Builder a few years ago that I figured I could try messing around with YAML code and a BME280 sensor module I’d bought for my Raspberry Pi eons ago. Not only did this experiment turn out successful, but I got so engrossed with it that I began populating my smart home with several other ESP32-powered sensor projects.

I wasted money on a Raspberry Pi when an $8 ESP32 could run half my DIY projects

I wish someone told me to start with an ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi

4
By  Ayush Pande

A weather station seemed like a novice project, but it turned out to be quite useful

The temperature metrics serve as reliable triggers for my automations

On the surface, a DIY temperature-monitoring setup seems more like a beginner-friendly project that has no utility outside of getting newcomers accustomed to the ESP32’s quirks… and that’s low-key what I thought when I sat down to work on this project. However, I quickly changed my mind when I got the BME280 module hooked up to my ESP32.

This might be a me problem, but it’s really hard to get the right temperature readings for the backwater town where I live. A general report of the surrounding city isn’t all that accurate, especially when the weather gets extremely turbulent. This wasn’t really a problem for me before I jumped down the Home Assistant rabbit hole. But since I wanted to create automation pipelines centered around precise temperature statistics, I couldn’t just import some random weather API and have it tweak my air-conditioning (and heating, depending on the season) using incorrect metrics.

Now, my BME280 sensor isn’t the most accurate at measuring temps, as its precision value is ±1.0°C, but it’s still good enough for my automation projects, especially since it has a neat trick up its sleeve. Compared to the likes of DHT11, DHT22, and other cheap temperature sensors, the BME280 can refresh the weather statics in milliseconds, making it perfect for a DIY matrix LED display that updates its temp metrics every second. As for automations, I’ve already configured my HVAC setup to use the stats pulled by my BME280 + ESP32 combo.

But my smart home also relies on humidity-sensing capabilities

Besides the temperature metrics, the BME280 can also scan the humidity values. For the longest time, I simply had my matrix LED setup show the humidity numbers but didn’t know what to do with them. However, once I began working with PETG models, the humidity-sensing capabilities of my DIY weather station became a clutch.

You see, PETG and a bunch of other filaments are hygroscopic, meaning they have a tendency to absorb moisture. This, in turn, can cause extra stringing when I turn them into tangible models, so I’d have to keep them as dry as possible. So, I created a second BME280 sensor specifically for my attic, which notifies me as soon as it detects the humidity level hitting the red zone. That way, I can unmount all the semi-used PETG filaments from my Elegoo CC2’s AMS module and keep them tucked inside a box full of silica gel.

4 simple ESP32 projects you can build without any sensors

Not all ESP32 projects need to involve extra sensors or circuit components

By  Ayush Pande

My successful weather station pushed me to presence detection sensors

The right sensors work well with lighting automations

One of the best aspects of ESP32 boards (and by extension, sensors) is their dirt-cheap pricing, and that’s pretty much why I was able to go out and buy a second one just for my 3D printing filaments. And well, I ended up grabbing a couple more ESP32-WROOM boards alongside whatever cool sensors met my fancy.

This includes the HC-SR501, which I promptly used to build trigger action rules dependent on human presence. But since this sensor can detect movement, it causes my presence-based automations to fail every time I sit in a room for long periods. So, I ended up grabbing an mmWave to light up my hallways and rooms even when I’m not scampering all over the place. Connecting both sensors to my ESP32 was a cakewalk, and just like the BME280, I simply followed the official ESPHome docs to get everything running on Home Assistant.

And things were never the same once I picked up a cheap box of sensors

Since I already had a handful of sensors by this point, I decided to go all out and bought a sensor collection. I’ll admit that a couple of the sensors were low-quality ones, but being able to mess with over 30 modules more than made up for this issue. So far, I’ve had some neat automation pipelines configured from the KY-022 IR receiver, KY-037 (and KY-038) sound sensor, KY-002 vibration detector, and a bunch of other modules, and I’m planning to work with the laser, metal touch, and heartbeat sensors over the weekend.

item.title: I finally discovered Roku’s secret menus and can’t believe what I was missing
item.itunes:title: I finally discovered Roku’s secret menus and can’t believe what I was missing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Among the mainstream streaming platforms, Roku is the least complicated. It might not be the prettiest or least clunky, but it's the most straightforward to use and least customizable. However, I found more beneath the basic UI than I expected once I started exploring its hidden menus. The menus let me do more than launch apps and watch streaming content.

I can access many menus, from developer options to other hidden menus beneath the main experience. Accessing the menus is like cheat codes in gaming, where you press a specific button combination on the controller. But instead of a controller, you press the buttons on the Roku remote.

Roku's hidden screens

There are more options than you think

I figured I had a handle on my Roku device's straightforward menu system. I have a Roku HD stick, and I've used a Roku Ultra in the past, which I have since given to my mom as a straightforward streaming experience. However, more options lurk beneath the clunky interface than I expected. The hidden Roku menus include options for app developers, engineers, discovering app versions, and troubleshooting.

Once I discovered these secret menus, I started digging into them. There are more Roku options than I realized, and I was surprised by what I'd been missing. I'm not a coder, so the developer screen wasn't much of an interest, but others let me troubleshoot apps and connectivity, do soft reboots, and much more.

This sideloaded Android Auto app is my favorite way to watch YouTube and browse the web in my car

Xtream Player is one of the more reliable options I've founded

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Secret reset screen

Find device details and factory reset options

This first menu lets you reset and update your device. A Soft Factory Reset reloads Roku software without completely wiping your account and Wi-Fi configuration. The Factory Reset option does what you would expect — erase everything and return it to factory settings. The USB Test option checks whether the Roku can detect and communicate with a USB drive if you have a port. For instance, I have a Roku Ultra that includes a USB-A port.

The SWUP option is aimed at developers and engineers. It changes the server endpoint Roku OS uses for staged update deployments and Roku devices' support diagnostics, but it doesn't get your device updates sooner. This is an interesting menu, but you shouldn't access it unless Roku support tells you to.

To access the secret reset screen, press the following button combination on the remote: Home 5 times > Fast Forward 3 times > Rewind two times.

I turned off this hidden Roku TV setting and reclaimed my privacy

Don't overlook this hidden privacy setting on Roku, which monitors OTA viewing activity.

By  Brian Burgess

Hidden channel info

Discover which app version you're running

Most of the time, a Roku will update apps in the background without you doing anything. However, sometimes the mechanism doesn't work, so the Roku ends up running the wrong app version. There could also be bugs in a particular app version that I need to troubleshoot. In any case, it can help to know which version of an app is running on your Roku.

That is when you can turn to the hidden channel (Roku calls apps channels) information screen, where you can see exactly which version of an app is running on your Roku. This information can help if you're troubleshooting an app or trying to figure out why the app on your Roku doesn't have the features you expect. If you have a lot of apps, the list will be long, and you'll need to scroll down to the right one.

To locate the hidden channel info screen, press the following button combination on the remote: Home 3 times > Up 2 times > Left > Right > Left > Right > Left.

I bought a Roku to keep things simple, and now I regret my decision

Roku offers an easy streaming, but ads are overwhelming and customization plans are ruined.

19
By  Brian Burgess

Hidden developer menu

You probably don't need it, but it's cool to look at

There are actually a few different hidden developer menu screens, but you likely don't need them unless you actually create and test apps on a Roku. Still, it's interesting to look at, and I even went so far as to sign up as a developer on the Roku website. However, if you aren't a developer, I don't advise making any changes; it's just interesting to look at.

If you are a developer, the menu lets you enable the developer installer and sideload apps on your Roku. It also lets you sign up for and manage the Roku Dev user account. But if you don't know how to code or what you're doing, leave all the settings in this hidden menu alone.

On your remote, press this button combination: Home 5 times > Up two times > Right > Left > Right > Left > Right.

I replaced my Roku with an old Android phone and haven't looked back

I turned my phone into a mobile Roku.

1
By  Brian Burgess

Hidden Screen 2

Manage annoying ads displayed throughout the Roku interface

This hidden screen lets me change how ads appear on the Roku's screensaver, change image formats, and even turn off screensaver ads entirely, depending on the model and Roku OS version the device is running. It lets me change image services, ad banner layout, manage screenshot output, and more.

This screen is powerful but tricky to use unless you know which settings you are configuring. I changed one setting at a time, went to the home screen to see what happened, then went back to adjust other ad placements. I couldn't turn off screens because I am running a new Roku HD stick with the latest version of Roku OS. Still, it's fun to play around with.

To access Secret Screen 2, press this remote combination: Home 5 times > Up > Right > Down > Left > Up.

Fox's Roku acquisition was the final push I needed to switch to the Apple TV 4K

Fox buying Roku will ruin the device even more, so I ditched it for Apple TV 4K.

20
By  Brian Burgess

Secret network settings

See connectivity data and test signal strength

If I'm having connectivity problems with my Roku stick, I can check the hidden network screen. I can view signal strength, antenna information, glitch rate, and logs; run a speed test; and reset the network. From this screen, I can also reset only the network to get a fresh start on my Wi-Fi.

I often access this screen if my picture is buffering, freezing, or not playing at all. Or maybe the picture quality isn't what it should be, or I can't install apps. I can check this screen for signal glitch rates, reset the Roku's wireless settings, and reconnect to my network to improve connectivity.

To access the Wireless Secret Screen, press the following combination on your remote: Home 5 times > Up > Down > Up > Down > Up.

Jellyfin's Roku app just got good enough to ditch Plex

The bugs are gone too, it's safe to upgrade

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Hidden Roku screen for everyone

I thought that I knew where everything was on Roku until I discovered its secret menus. I can do a lot with them to help troubleshoot apps, Wi-Fi connectivity, and more. It would be nice if they weren't hidden. The company probably thinks users will screw up their TVs, sticks, or boxes. However, adding the secret screens to an "advanced" section of the normal menu system would be nice, sans developer settings.

item.title: I stopped using cloud smart bulbs after finding Zigbee local control, and my automations never fail anymore
item.itunes:title: I stopped using cloud smart bulbs after finding Zigbee local control, and my automations never fail anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you swap over to a smart home, it doesn't really feel like an upgrade when you're standing in the dark for 3 to 5 seconds while your smart bulbs think about turning on.

It's so easy to start your smart home journey with cheap colorful Wi-Fi smart bulbs. They seem great out of the box, but realistically they clutter your router's DHCP table, saturate your 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels, and tether every single color change and automation to a corporate AWS server halfway across the country.

Ripping out every single Wi-Fi cloud bulb and replacing them with standard Zigbee 3.0 bulbs tied to a local coordinator allows you to decouple your home from corporate servers, eliminate wireless latency, and build an air-gapped lighting system that executes automations instantaneously and never fails.

7 ESP32 projects that replaced commercial smart home gadgets in my house with cheaper, local hardware

These are the commercial products I've replaced with ESP32-powered variants.

11
By  Adam Conway

You're causing issues with your network

And your bulb takes ages to switch on

Wi-Fi smart bulbs essentially destroy your home network. This is because they require a full network stack, including IP assignment, DHCP handshakes, TLS handshakes, and keep-alive packets, just to toggle a light on or off. That doesn't sound like much with a single bulb, but with 30 to 40 Wi-Fi smart devices actively beaming on your home 2.4 GHz spectrum, it can create massive co-channel interference and degrade your router's performance for your main devices (like your laptops, phones, and streaming boxes).

There's also the cloud round-trip penalty because the path of a simple cloud automation goes from the motion sensor to the vendor cloud app to an AWS server in Virginia to a vendor API to your local router and then to your Wi-Fi bulb. Every link in that chain adds latency, jitter, and potential failure points. If any single microservice goes down, your light switch essentially stops working.

There's also the risk of your hardware becoming e-waste if there is firmware abandonment. Consumer cloud bulb manufacturers treat firmware maintenance as an afterthought. Remember, they release a newer hardware revision and older bulbs can be abandoned to security vulnerabilities and broken integrations. The product you've spent money on and installed in your home can become obsolete in a second.

The technology behind Zigbee

How exactly does Zigbee work?

Zigbee feels like a revolution once you've spent so long using cloud-based smart home products. This is because you get sub-second local mesh intelligence. Instead of bulky IP packets, Zigbee passes tiny raw 25- to 127-byte data frames over local hardware addresses directly to a local USB coordinator. There are no cloud roundtrips or TLS handshakes and no external WAN dependencies.

There's also the benefit of the self-healing mesh topology. Unlike Wi-Fi endpoints that all compete to talk directly to a distant router, mains-powered Zigbee bulbs act as an active routing node or repeater. The more Zigbee lights you install, the denser and more robust your home's mesh network becomes. A bulb across the house passes packets along a multi-hop mesh path instantly.

You also get the benefit of universal interoperability. Unlike a lot of Wi-Fi-based products, any certified Zigbee 3.0 bulb pairs natively with any open coordinator like Home Assistant, Hubitat, ZHA, or Zigbee2MQTT without ever needing a vendor app or an account sign-up. Your phone doesn't need to be clogged with third-party apps just to control all the devices in your smart home.

Your automations will finally feel smart

As well as a range of other benefits

The real-world payoff is unbreakable, reliable automations throughout your home. Execution is instantaneous due to the fact that it's local. You get a sub-50ms motion trigger. Walking into a dark hallway triggers a Zigbee motion sensor that talks directly to the local coordinator, which instantly fires the Zigbee bulb group. The light turns on before your foot crosses the threshold, matching the feel of a hardwired mechanical switch.

Instead of waiting for a cloud-based round trip, you also get rid of the trickle-down lighting effect. In a lot of cloud setups, turning on a group of six ceiling lights can result in a ragged popcorn effect as commands trickle down sequentially over the internet. Local Zigbee multicast groups allow a single broadcast frame to toggle dozens of bulbs simultaneously in exact unison. It doesn't feel like you're waiting for each bulb to turn on one by one, and you also get seamless manual override harmony.

Because local Zigbee bulbs don't lose smart functionality when toggled via physical wall switches (when paired with smart modules or decoupled switch states), guests and family members can still use the physical switches without breaking automation states, the way that occurs with cloud-based devices.

You shouldn't have to spend time waiting for your lights to turn on

A smart home should be smart

Smart lighting was never meant to be a cloud service, and turning on a light bulb shouldn't leave you waiting in the dark for up to five seconds. Instead, turning on a light bulb should feel like a fundamental household utility that should function with the same reliability as indoor plumbing, independent of whether your internet is working or a tech startup's servers are online. By replacing cloud Wi-Fi bulbs with local Zigbee alternatives, you can experience the speed, privacy, and absolute reliability of a truly local smart home.

item.title: After five years of early access, Valheim finally lets you rebind the dodge button
item.itunes:title: After five years of early access, Valheim finally lets you rebind the dodge button
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Valheim now lets you rebind the dodge key - no more holding right-click + Space or using mods.
  • Patch 1.0.14 adds QoL: rebind 1–8, remove binds, radial wheel changes, toggle blocking, skip intro.
  • After five years of early access, 1.0 finally makes Valheim the game it always aimed to be.

Good things come to those who wait, which is excellent news for people who have been waiting patiently for an official way to rebind the dodge button in the newly launched title Valheim. Despite the game undergoing five years of early access, the devs have finally added a way to change what you press to dodge an incoming attack.

Valheim's newest update adds a feature people had to previously mod in

Better late than never

Credit: Iron Gate AB

As PC Gamer has spotted, Valheim has received a few updates since its grand release. While the game's v1.0 badge is brand new, it spent five years in early access, and yet it took this long to finally add a way to change the dodge key to something else. It got so bad that people were developing macros and mods simply to rebind the dodge button to something other than holding right-click and pressing Space while holding a direction.

In fact, the entire 'Quality of Life' section in the patch notes for version 1.0.14 sounds like a delight. You can rebind the 1-8 keys, remove keybinds, and change the binds for the radial wheel. There's a new accessibility option that lets you toggle blocking instead of holding down a key, and there's a new setting that will auto-skip the intro. Fantastic stuff. Oh, and if you fancy taking Valheim wherever you want, the new patch adds "Multiple GPU performance improvements on Switch 2," which is always nice.

If you're still on the fence about jumping back into this Viking delight, Tomas Franzese on our lovely sister site Polygon has been gushing about how Valheim’s 1.0 update is finally the game it was always meant to be.

Some essential, and not-so-essential upgrades.
